title: Brigade-and-below multinational SA/C2 bridge and releasability-aware coalition COP federation (productized Mission Partner Kit with partner-specific views and federated partner identity across TAK, SitaWare and national systems)
problem: U.S. and allied units at brigade and below cannot quickly and lawfully share positions, geometries, chat and voice across national C2 systems, so regiments build ad hoc cloud kits, partners are managed as guests on separate enclaves, and release decisions still run through liaison officers, translation gateways and manual sanitization rather than releasability-tagged objects and federated partner identities.

current_workflow: Allied unit arrives with its national BMS (SitaWare, FC BISA, TOPAZ, national fire-control system) and national radios; U.S. unit runs TAK/Nett Warrior, CPCE/SitaWare HQ and national Secret enclaves.
A U.S. LNO physically embeds with the partner carrying a Mission Partner Kit laptop/phone or TAK device; a partner LNO reciprocates.
If cloud/commercial connectivity exists, positions and chat are exchanged through a cloud-hosted SBU kit or a mission-partner network; if not, by voice and radio relay.
Battlefield geometries and fire-support coordination measures are re-entered by hand in each national system because geometry discipline and C2IS-to-fire-control interfaces differ.

Products generated on U.S. collateral Secret systems are reviewed by an FDO, regenerated or re-marked REL on the MPE lower enclave with a different tool, and pushed through an accredited cross-domain solution.
Partner users receive nationally issued guest accounts on each coalition enclave; account changes propagate by email/ticket; U.S. staff swivel between national and coalition terminals.

At exercise start (Bold Quest, CWIX, Balikatan, Warfighter) integrators spend weeks configuring ASCA/NFFI/NVG gateways and JICOs hand-tag data so it can pass the CDS; the configuration decays after the event.
current_solution: Government-owned TAK (ATAK/WinTAK/TAK Server with federation), Systematic SitaWare HQ/Frontline/Edge (native NFFI/NVG/MIP, NATO DEMETER incumbent), Army CPCE built on SitaWare, unit-built 2CR Mission Partner Kit (SBU, commercial cloud, COTS), Army Coalition Interoperability Solution (ACIS, 2018 urgent need), ASCA fires gateways, DISA MPE enclaves (CENTRIXS, Pegasus, CFBLNet, APAN) run by Trace Systems under MPE-S and by SOSi/GDIT under network-engineering task orders, INDOPACOM Mission Network (zero-trust, first tested May 2026), Booz Allen Sit(x) bridging Lattice to TAK/partner systems, Mattermost with ABAC channels as MPE chat, Microsoft Entra B2B guest identities, accredited CDS from Everfox/Owl/GDMS, and human LNOs and FDOs as the actual release mechanism.
failure: Releasability is not a first-class attribute on COP objects and partner identity is not federated, so enforcement happens by enclave (network) rather than by object; anything produced on a national Secret system without REL markings cannot flow and is regenerated or re-keyed; geometry and fires data break at national interfaces; kits are cloud-dependent and unit-owned rather than programs of record; DISA itself says MPE stays network-centric until about 2027 and that partner networks are 'consolidated stovepipes'.

why_existing_startups_havent_solved: The binding constraints are policy and accreditation, not code: data created on national Secret systems without REL markings cannot legally flow, so the release decision is owned by FDOs and national disclosure policy; every enclave and guard needs its own accreditation (NCDSMO Raise-the-Bar) and the accredited CDS market is an oligopoly (Everfox, Owl, GDMS, Northrop). On the unclassified/SBU side the substrate is free and government-owned (TAK, with federation built in), the allied incumbent (Systematic SitaWare) already speaks NFFI/NVG/MIP natively and is NATO's DEMETER land C2, and the services layer is locked up in large IDIQs (Trace Systems MPE-S $998M ceiling, GDIT EMITS 2 $1.25B ceiling, SOSi mission-network engineering) where bridges are delivered as labor, not product. No single buyer owns brigade-level coalition interoperability (units, USAREUR-AF, DISA, Joint Staff J6, NATO ACT/NCIA and national MoDs each own a piece), so urgent-need kits (ACIS 2018, MPK 2024) never became programs of record and there is no SBIR/RFI demand signal for a product. Startups that came close (Hadean, Immersive Wisdom, Raft, Second Front) sell adjacent layers (wargaming, DDIL collaboration, data federation, ATO hosting) rather than the releasability/identity core, which requires cleared U.S. staff and multinational agreements a small team cannot obtain.
technical_wedge: An unclassified-first, DDIL-tolerant 'coalition edge broker' that runs on a laptop or phone without cloud dependency and (1) federates TAK Server / ATAK feeds with SitaWare-compatible NFFI/NVG/ADatP-3 and MIP-lite outputs with store-and-forward sync, (2) attaches a NATO-label-style releasability attribute (ACP-240 / STANAG 4774-4778 confidentiality metadata) to every CoT/COP object at creation and computes partner-specific COP views from a policy file an FDO can read and sign, (3) validates battlefield-geometry conformance before export so fires geometries survive national interfaces, and (4) brokers partner identity through SAML/OIDC federation with attribute mapping so guest accounts are not hand-provisioned per enclave. It deliberately stops at the SBU/Secret-releasable boundary and hands objects to an accredited CDS via well-formed metadata, positioning as the offline, product-shaped counterpart to unit-built Mission Partner Kits and to labor-delivered MPE bridges.

mvp.what: Two simulated 'nations' each running a TAK Server (nation A) and a SitaWare-compatible NFFI/NVG endpoint or open MIP-style emulator (nation B) connected through the broker over an intermittent link; every object carries a releasability label; each nation sees only its permitted view; an FDO console shows the policy, an audit log and what was withheld; geometry conformance checks flag malformed fire-support coordination measures before export.
mvp.demonstrable_in_3_6_months: Yes for the TAK-to-TAK federation with labels, per-partner views, DDIL store-and-forward and audit; the SitaWare side can only be emulated from public STANAG/NFFI/NVG schemas unless Systematic or an allied MoD grants interface access; identity federation via Keycloak/Entra test tenants is feasible in the window.
mvp.what_it_must_prove: That per-object releasability plus partner-specific views can be set up in hours instead of weeks, survive a disconnected period without leaking or losing objects, produce an audit an FDO accepts, and pass a CWIX Innovation Sandbox or Bold Quest-style conformance test against real national systems - not just that two TAK servers can talk (they already can).

data_requirement.what: Public NATO/FMN standards (NFFI STANAG 5527, NVG, ADatP-3, MIP/JC3IEDM and MIM, ACP-240 and STANAG 4774/4778 labeling), the open-source ATAK-CIV/TAK Server code and CoT schema, synthetic multinational scenarios, and later CUI exercise data (partner attribute schemas, disclosure-policy encodings) obtained through an exercise sponsor.
data_requirement.legally_realistically_obtainable: Standards and ATAK-CIV are public (TAK-GOV/MIL builds are distribution-controlled); synthetic data is unlimited; real disclosure-policy encodings and partner attribute schemas are mostly controlled or classified and only obtainable inside a sponsored exercise (CWIX Innovation Sandbox, Bold Quest, Bundeswehr/NATO battle lab). A non-U.S.-person founder can work on the public/synthetic tier; access to U.S. CUI or export-controlled interface data requires counsel review.

entry_vehicle.primary: Allied-first: NATO DIANA challenge cohort or CWIX Innovation Sandbox participation with a Bundeswehr or NATO sponsor, using the Rapid Adoption Action Plan (June 2025) path from prototype to procurement; U.S. entry as a TAK plugin / team-member app rather than a prime
sequence: 0-3 months: counsel on entity structure (U.S. Inc. vs German GmbH vs dual), export classification, SBIR ownership test, and a written plan for the non-U.S.-person founder's data access
0-6 months: build the unclassified TAK-to-TAK labeled federation MVP on ATAK-CIV; register SAM/CAGE; submit a Tradewinds video for 'awardable' status

3-9 months: apply to NATO DIANA (next challenge call) and request CWIX Innovation Sandbox or Bundeswehr Cyber Innovation Hub sponsorship; approach Systematic or a national C2 vendor for interface access as a partner

6-12 months: pursue an Army xTech (xTechSearch/xTechPacific) entry if the cap table meets the SBIR test, and a USAREUR-AF or INDOPACOM J6 exercise trial through an existing integrator (GDIT EMITS 2, SOSi, Booz Allen) as a subcontracted product
12-24 months: Bold Quest / CWIX conformance evidence -> NCIA or national MoD procurement via Rapid Adoption Service; U.S. follow-on as a CPE C2IN C2-Enablers or DISA CIE plug-in via prototype OT/CSO
24+ months: only then consider a facility clearance and FOCI mitigation to touch Secret-releasable enclaves
entry_vehicle.eligibility_notes: SBIR/STTR requires >50% ownership and control by U.S. citizens or permanent residents (13 CFR 121.702); the German founder counts only once a green card is granted and the Indonesian founder does not, so SBIR is closed until the cap table is restructured (counsel). AFWERX open topics restrict foreign-national participation to public-domain work and require U.S. performance. OTA/CSO/xTech prize routes have no statutory ownership test but export-controlled CUI and ITAR technical data are effectively U.S.-person-only, and any facility clearance triggers FOCI review where a permanent resident is still a 'foreign interest' (32 CFR 117.11). NATO DIANA and German channels are open to the German founder; EU EDF/EDIP instruments are constrained by third-country control rules. None of this is a legal determination - it requires export-control and immigration counsel.

incumbent_response.could_anduril_palantir_l3harris_add_it: Yes for the U.S. side: Anduril (NGC2 data layer lead) and Palantir (Maven NATO, Army EA) can add releasability attributes and partner views inside their platforms and already sit in the coalition exercises (PCC6 with NZ/AUS/UK/CA partners, Maven at Steadfast exercises); Systematic can do the same on the allied side; the MPE integrators can hire the capability under existing task orders. The one piece they do not want to own is the cross-vendor, cross-nation neutral broker plus the FDO-facing policy workflow, because each incumbent wants its own platform to be the spine.
incumbent_response.why_startup_still_wins_or_reject: A startup wins only if it is the neutral, standards-native, DDIL-tolerant broker that allied nations and NATO bodies trust precisely because it is not Anduril, Palantir or Systematic, and if it enters through NATO/German channels where the incumbents' U.S. ELAs do not reach. In the U.S. market alone the honest call is REJECT as a standalone company: the government-owned TAK plus unit-built kits are 'good enough' at SBU, the valuable Secret-releasable and cross-domain part is closed to a non-cleared, mixed-nationality team, and there is no product demand signal. As an allied-first product with a later U.S. plug-in path it is a defensible but narrow business.

regulatory_burden.explanation: Unclassified TAK/standards work carries only DFARS 252.204-7012/CMMC and possibly EAR 5D002 encryption obligations, but any move to Secret-releasable data, MPE enclaves or cross-domain hand-off requires accredited hosting (IL5/IL6 or NATO Secret), authorization evidence (SWFT/cATO or NATO ATO), FMN/JITC conformance, and cleared staff; the release policy itself is government-owned, so the company depends on FDO/disclosure-authority acceptance it cannot control. Foreign investment into an ITAR/600-series product can trigger mandatory CFIUS declarations. These are descriptions of constraints, not legal conclusions - counsel required.
regulatory_burden.non_us_person_founder_note: The Indonesian founder (not a U.S. person) can lawfully work on public-domain standards, open-source ATAK-CIV and synthetic data; access to ITAR technical data or export-controlled CUI would need a license/TAA or must be walled off; a German lawful permanent resident is a U.S. person for ITAR (22 CFR 120.62) but still a 'foreign interest' for FOCI and cannot hold a clearance without citizenship; SBIR's >50% U.S.-person ownership test likely fails on the current cap table; a dual U.S./German structure raises German AWG/EU dual-use obligations in the other direction. Counsel must design the entity, data-segregation plan and hiring policy before any U.S. government engagement.

dual_use_potential.explanation: The same label-aware, DDIL-tolerant federation and partner-identity brokering applies to multinational disaster response and humanitarian coordination (TAK is widely used by civil agencies), cross-agency public safety, border and coast-guard cooperation, and critical-infrastructure operators sharing incident pictures under NDA-like rules; the commercial market is real but thin and lower-priced, and the releasability semantics are specifically military.

defensibility.explanation: Nothing algorithmic is defensible (labels, federation and policy engines are standards-based); the moat would be the tested adapter set against dozens of national systems, exercise-proven conformance evidence, FDO-accepted policy workflow, authorizations that others must repeat, and the trust of being neutral across Anduril/Palantir/Systematic spines. That moat is slow to build and easily undercut by incumbents bundling a 'good enough' bridge for free.

why_now: Since 2023 the coalition C2 problem moved from theater HQs to brigade level and from talk to funded programs: NGC2 fielding with multinational partners at PCC6 (2026), Army Jailbreak expansion to foreign partners (planned 2026), DISA's Coalition Information Environment and INDOPACOM Mission Network proof-outs (2026) with a stated network-centric-to-data-centric pivot by ~2027, Thunderdome extension to mission partners, the DoD zero-trust target date (FY2027) forcing data tagging and ICAM, NATO's DEMETER (SitaWare FOC 2026), Maven NATO (2025) and the Rapid Adoption Action Plan (June 2025) plus DIANA's Rapid Adoption Service (Dec 2025), the 5%-of-GDP pledge lifting allied C4ISR budgets, and TAK's spread to 500k+ users across partner nations creating a common substrate. At the same time the FY27 request steers joint C2 money into Maven/JFN licenses, which narrows the startup's U.S. lane to plug-ins.
killer_risk: Policy, not technology, is the bottleneck and the technology part is already commoditized: national disclosure rules and FDO judgment decide what can be shared, the SBU bridge is handled 'well enough' by free government TAK plus unit kits and by SitaWare's native standards, the valuable Secret-releasable and cross-domain layer is closed to a non-cleared mixed-nationality team, no buyer has issued a product RFI or SBIR topic in eight years of recurring urgent needs, and incumbents (Anduril/Palantir in NGC2 and Maven, Systematic in NATO, MPE integrators under $1B-ceiling IDIQs) can bundle the capability for free the moment a customer asks - leaving a thin, exercise-dependent services business rather than a product company.

Oversight and allied buys: GAO-25-106454 (Apr); NCIA buys Maven NATO sole-source (Mar); DEMETER SitaWare IOC (Mar); DODIG-2025-126 released (Jul); Bold Quest 25 and CWIX25 (Jun); GDIT EMITS 2 incl. mission partner network (Sep, $1.25B ceiling); NATO Rapid Adoption Action Plan (Jun)

Proof-outs, not products: DISA CIE testing in INDOPACOM (Jun) and 'network-centric until ~2027' (Aug); INDOPACOM Mission Network first test and eight-nation COP at Balikatan (May); NGC2 common data baseline (Jun) and PCC6 with NZ/AUS/UK/CA partners (Aug); FY27 budget funds CIE hybrid-cloud MPE (Apr)

allied_extension: Yes - this is the one gap in the study where the allied market is more open than the U.S. market. NATO and European nations run SitaWare/FMN-native C2, buy through NCIA/NSPA and national MoDs that are reforming for speed (Rapid Adoption Action Plan 2025, DIANA Rapid Adoption Service, Allied Innovation Procurement Forum 2026), fund CWIX participation, and lack the U.S. classified-enclave lock-in; a German founder can enter via DIANA, the CWIX Innovation Sandbox and the Bundeswehr Cyber Innovation Hub without SBIR ownership problems, and the AUKUS ITAR exemption and Five Eyes Overmatch agreement create additional bilateral lanes. The counterweights are that Systematic already owns the allied land-C2 spine, Palantir owns NATO's theater platform, EU EDF/EDIP instruments are constrained by third-country control, and multinational disclosure policy is even more fragmented than U.S. policy; the allied version of this business is more compelling but still an integration-and-conformance business rather than a scalable product.
